summary:
Paul wrote Romans around AD 57, near the end of his third missionary journey, to a church he had never visited. He was planning to stop in Rome on his way to a new mission field in Spain, and this letter is his introduction: the fullest, most ordered account of the gospel he preached anywhere in his writings. That completeness is why Romans has carried unusual weight in church history; Augustine, Luther, and Barth each traced a turning point in their thinking to it.

Read it as a single argument. Chapters 1-3 build the case that everyone, Gentile and Jew alike, stands guilty before God, then pivot on the letter's hinge: "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" (3:23-24). "Justified" is a courtroom word, meaning declared in the right with God, and Paul's claim is that it comes by faith, as a gift, not by keeping the Law.

Chapters 5-8 trace the new life that follows: Adam's sin answered by Christ's obedience, baptism as dying and rising with Christ, a frank account of ongoing moral struggle in chapter 7, and the promise at the height of chapter 8 that nothing in all creation "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Chapters 9-11 face the question that grieved Paul most personally: why have so many of his fellow Jews not believed in their Messiah? The closing chapters (12-16) turn to practice, opening with "offer your bodies as living sacrifices" (12:1). Notice how each instruction there leans on the argument that came before it; the theology is never left abstract.
